prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Once I believed in you; I planted a fig tree. Here, in Vermont, country of no summer. It was a test: if the tree lived, it would mean you existed. By this logic, you do not exist. Or you exist exclusively in warmer climates, in fervent Sicily and Mexico and California, where are grown the unimaginable apricot and fragile peach. Perhaps they see your face in Sicily; here we barely see the hem of your garment. I have to discipline myself to share with John and Noah the tomato crop. If there is justice in some other world, those like myself, whom nature forces into lives of abstinence, should get the lion's share of all things, all objects of hunger, greed being praise of you. And no one praises more intensely than I, with more painfully checked desire, or more deserves to sit at your right hand, if it exists, partaking of the perishable, the immortal fig, which does not travel.

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your text:

---

Once, I believed in you, and so I planted a fig tree—here, in Vermont, this country of no summer. It was a test: if the tree survived, it would prove that you existed. By that logic, you do not. Or perhaps you exist only in warmer climates—in fervent Sicily, in Mexico and California, where the unimaginable apricot and the fragile peach are grown. Perhaps in Sicily they behold your very face; here, we scarcely glimpse the hem of your garment. I must discipline myself to share the tomato crop with John and Noah.

If there is justice in some other world, then those like me—whom nature condemns to lives of abstinence—should receive the lion's share of all things, of every object of hunger, since greed itself is a form of praise for you. And no one praises more intensely than I do, with desire more painfully restrained; no one more deserves to sit at your right hand, should it exist, partaking of the perishable, the immortal fig, which does not travel.

---

A note: this passage is, in fact, Louise Glück's poem "Vespers" from her Pulitzer Prize–winning collection *The Wild Iris* (1992). I've refined it toward smoother, more formal prose as requested, but you may wish to preserve the original, given its literary provenance. Let me know if you'd like a different approach.
outputs.L2: There was a time I trusted you; so I set a fig tree in the ground. Right here in Vermont, a land where summer never truly arrives. I meant it as a trial: should the tree survive, that would prove you were real. Following that reasoning, then, you are not real. Or maybe you dwell only where the weather stays mild—in passionate Sicily, in Mexico, in California, places that produce the inconceivable apricot and the delicate peach. It may be that in Sicily they glimpse your countenance; over here we scarcely catch sight of the edge of your robe. I must force myself to divide the tomato harvest with John and Noah. Should justice exist in some other realm, then people such as me—those whom nature compels toward lives of going without—ought to receive the greatest portion of everything, every thing we hunger for, since to crave is to worship you. And nobody worships with greater fervor than I do, nobody with desire more agonizingly restrained, nobody more worthy of a place at your right side, should such a place be real, feeding on that which spoils, the undying fig, the fruit that cannot be carried away.
outputs.L3:
# On God, Climate, and the Fig Tree

I once planted a fig tree in Vermont, intending it as a kind of experiment—a test of whether God truly exists. When the tree failed to survive the harsh northern winter, I took its death as evidence that God does not exist, or at the very least, does not dwell in cold climates.

It seems to me that God may only be present in warmer regions—places like Sicily, Mexico, and California, where rich fruits flourish under a generous sun. In such lands, where the earth yields its sweetness freely, people can perceive the divine more directly, as if abundance itself were a form of revelation.

But those of us who live in harsh climates are forced into a different existence altogether—one of abstinence and scarcity. Here, even the modest tomato crop demands discipline, and it takes genuine effort to share what little grows with others. Ours is a life shaped by deprivation rather than plenty.

And yet I would argue that this very deprivation carries its own strange dignity. Those who are denied life's pleasures by nature herself surely deserve the greatest share of desirable things. In this light, greed and hunger become their own forms of praise—expressions of longing that honor the very abundance we are denied.

Indeed, I claim to praise God most intensely of all, precisely through the pain of restrained desire. My hunger is my worship. And so I believe I deserve a place of honor, and above all, access to that fragile, immortal fig—the fruit so delicate that it cannot survive the journey to reach me, and so remains forever just beyond my grasp.
outputs.L4:
# The Fig Tree in Vermont

The poem opens with an image of quiet defeat: a fig tree, planted with hope in the stubborn soil of Vermont, has failed to survive. Figs belong to warmer countries—to the Mediterranean, to the lands of scripture where such trees appear in parable and promise. But here, in the granite hills of the north, the speaker has attempted something the climate will not permit. The tree stands blackened by frost, its branches bare, its intended fruit never formed. This small agricultural tragedy becomes the seed from which the entire meditation grows.

From this failure, the speaker constructs a stark and almost bitter theology. If God exists, the reasoning goes, then God dwells where the fig tree thrives—in the sun-warmed south, among olive groves and vineyards, in the biblical landscapes of abundance. The cold northern regions, by this logic, are territories God has abandoned or never claimed. The dead tree becomes evidence in a private trial of faith: its inability to live proves either divine nonexistence or divine absence. Where there is no fruit, the speaker suggests, there is no God to bless the branches. The harsh climate is not merely inhospitable to figs but to grace itself.

Yet the poem does not remain in this place of accusation. As the meditation deepens, the speaker's argument turns and transforms into something unexpected. If the north is a place of deprivation—of short growing seasons, killing frosts, and hungers that cannot be satisfied—then perhaps those who endure such conditions are not the forsaken but the chosen. The people driven by nature into want, into restraint, into the discipline of doing without, may deserve the greatest reward of all. Their suffering is not punishment but a strange qualification for blessing.

Here the poem arrives at its central paradox. Physical hunger, the emptiness of the stomach and the barrenness of the land, becomes a form of prayer. The desire that must be restrained, the appetite that cannot be fed, transforms into spiritual longing—a reaching toward the divine that is more intense precisely because it goes unfulfilled. Those who have everything need nothing; those who have nothing are shaped entirely by their yearning. In this way, deprivation becomes its own kind of worship, and the ache of want becomes indistinguishable from the ache of faith.

The failed fig tree, then, is not simply proof of God's absence. It becomes a monument to a different theology altogether—one in which barrenness and cold, hunger and restraint, are not signs of abandonment but the very conditions under which the deepest spiritual longing can take root. The speaker's crisis of faith resolves not into certainty of God's presence or absence, but into an understanding that longing itself, born of scarcity, may be the truest and most human form of devotion.
outputs.L5:
# Once, Here in Vermont

*Once*, when the world felt too loud and the days blurred together, I found myself driving north until the highways surrendered to winding country roads. That was how I first came to Vermont.

*Here*, everything moves at a different pace. The mornings arrive wrapped in mist that clings to the Green Mountains, and the maple trees stretch endlessly across the hills like a patient, ancient forest that has watched generations come and go. There is a stillness in Vermont that you don't so much see as feel—a quiet that settles into your bones.

*Once* you've spent an autumn here, you understand why people fall in love with this place. The foliage erupts into impossible shades of crimson, amber, and gold. Farm stands line the roads, offering fresh cider, warm pumpkin bread, and jars of golden syrup tapped from the very trees around you.

*Here*, the seasons don't just pass; they announce themselves boldly. Winter blankets the countryside in deep, glittering snow. Spring brings the sweet rush of sap and the first tender green. Summer unfolds in wildflower meadows and cool, clear lakes.

*Once* a traveler, always a returning friend—that is what Vermont does to a person. It welcomes you slowly and then holds you completely.

So if you ever find yourself weary of the noise, come *here*. Come to Vermont, where time slows down, the air tastes clean, and *once* you arrive, you may never want to leave.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the voice of a gardener in Vermont addressing God, using a fig tree as a test of divine existence.
counterfactuals.output:
**Test of the Fig**

Lord, if You're there, then answer me in leaves.
I dragged this fig from Italy's warm blood
to Vermont ground, where every winter grieves
and forty below can turn the sap to mud.

They told me it would die. A Zone-4 fool,
they said, to plant a thing that dreams of Rome.
But I wrapped its trunk in burlap, kept it cool
in the cellar dark, and called that dark a home.

So here's my wager, plain as this cracked hand:
if come July it fruits against all sense,
against the frost, the odds, the frozen land—
I'll take that purple sweetness as Your evidence.

I don't ask much. No burning bush, no voice.
No parting of the Winooski's spring flood.
Just one ripe fig to prove the world's a choice
some Maker made, and made it out of love.

Or maybe You're the cold that kills the tree.
Maybe You're the summer that it needs.
Maybe You're neither—just the mystery
of why a man kneels down and plants his seeds

in soil that shouldn't hold them. Still I dig.
Still I wrap the roots and wait, and pray,
and watch the branch for one impossible fig—
and if it comes, I'll have my faith. I'll say

I told You so, old Silence. I'll say grace
over the fruit no reason should allow,
and know You by the sugar on my face.
And if it doesn't—Lord, I'm digging now.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem about faith, envy, and desire, framed around growing fruit in a cold northern climate.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Cold Teaches

I wanted figs.

Not the idea of figs—
the actual weight of them,
purple and splitting,
the way they grow easy in warmer countries
where women pull them from branches
without prayer.

Here, the ground stays locked
until May pretends at kindness.
I planted anyway.
This is what faith is:
burying something alive
in soil that has killed
everything before it.

I confess I have coveted
the orchards of the south,
their careless abundance,
the farmer who does nothing
and receives everything.
I have stood in my own thin rows
and felt the green sickness rise—
why them, why the ease,
why the fruit that falls
into open hands.

But desire is not the same as envy,
though they share a root.
Envy wants what another holds.
Desire only wants,
and keeps wanting,
and in the wanting
learns the shape of the wanted thing.

So I wrap the young trunks in burlap.
I carry water. I wait
through the long refusal of winter,
through the doubt that is not the absence of faith
but its actual body,
its cold and aching muscle.

And when the first fruit comes—
one, only one,
small as a child's fist,
sweet past all deserving—

I understand
the south has never tasted anything
this earned.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Louise Glück-style poem where the speaker bargains with God through gardening and questions whether God exists.
counterfactuals.output:
**Terms**

I gave you the tomatoes.
That was the first offering—
not the fruit but the labor,
my hands in the cold soil
before the soil was ready,
before I was ready to believe
anything would rise.

If you are there,
I said, let something rise.
And something did, though I know
the seed contains its own instruction,
its own quiet arithmetic
that does not require you.

Still, I bargain.
I stake the peas. I thin the lettuce.
I pull the weeds you did not plant
or planted carelessly,
the way a distracted father
scatters what he means to keep.

Here is my proposal:
I will kneel each morning.
I will forgive the frost.
And in return you will show me
one clear sign—not a miracle,
I am past miracles—
only a word, a small green certainty.

But the garden answers
the way the dead answer,
which is to say it thrives
and says nothing,
the beans indifferent as scripture,
the light arriving on schedule
whether or not I pray.

Perhaps this is the sign.
Perhaps the silence is the answer
and I, wanting the human voice,
have mistaken your presence
for your absence,
the way a child, left alone,
believes the whole house empty.

Or perhaps I am alone.
Either way, I keep the terms.
I turn the earth. I wait.
I offer you the tomatoes
and you take them
the way you take everything—
completely, and without a word.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a monologue addressed to a possibly-absent deity, contrasting the abundance of warm climates with the sparse harvest of Vermont.
counterfactuals.output:
**Monologue: On the Ledge of October**

*(A farmer stands at the edge of a stony field, a basket half-empty at his feet. The wind carries the first cold.)*

---

So. Here we are again. You and I—if there is a *you* at all, and not just the wind rehearsing my own voice back to me.

I've been told You are generous. I've read the accounts. I've heard the preachers describe Your open hand, how it spills over some corner of the world I'll never see. Somewhere south of here—somewhere You apparently *love*—there are trees so heavy with fruit the branches beg to be relieved of it. Oranges dropping into the grass like coins from a torn pocket. Bananas, figs, whole orchards that never learned the meaning of *November*. They tell me the ground there just *gives*. That a man can lie beneath a tree with his mouth open and be fed.

And I believe them. That's the terrible part. I believe You did that. I believe You knelt in that warm dirt and pressed abundance into it with Your thumb like a child making pies out of mud.

Then You came here.

You looked at Vermont—at these hills, at this granite masquerading as soil—and what did You think? Did You laugh? Did You set down Your basket of miracles and say, *this one gets the leftovers*? Because that's what I'm holding. Look at it. Look. A season of my back bent double, my hands split at the knuckle, and this is the yield. A few hard apples. Squash the frost has already threatened. Potatoes I dug like a man robbing his own grave.

I'm not asking for oranges. Understand me. I never asked to lie in the grass with my mouth open. I only asked that the ground meet me *halfway*. That's all. Halfway.

But maybe that's the joke, and maybe You're not even here to hear me tell it. Maybe You emptied Yourself into the tropics and had nothing left for the north but stone and a short summer and a long, instructive winter.

And yet.

*(He picks up an apple. Turns it in his hand.)*

And yet this one is sweeter. God help me—if You're there, help me—it *is*. The cold does something to it the warm places never could. Concentrates it. Makes it fight for its own flavor. Down south the fruit is lazy with sweetness; it never had to earn a thing. But this—this apple knew the frost was coming and decided to be sweet *anyway*, out of spite, out of stubbornness, out of some hard little northern faith I recognize because it is my own.

So here is what I think, standing on this ledge, talking to a sky that may hold nothing but weather:

Maybe You didn't give this place *less*. Maybe You gave it *hunger*, and hunger is the mother of everything I've ever loved. The people here don't lie in the grass. They stand up. They lean into the wind. They plant in stone and call it optimism.

I still don't know if You're listening. I've stopped expecting the sky to answer.

But I'll be back in the spring. On my knees in the cold mud, arguing with a God I can't prove, planting seeds in a ground that owes me nothing.

Call it faith. Call it stubbornness.

Up here, I've never been able to tell the difference.

*(He shoulders the basket. Walks toward the house as the light goes.)*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemplative poem about abstinence, greed, and worthiness, where a Vermont gardener resents having to share tomatoes and claims the fig as a sacred, immortal reward.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Fig-Keeper's Confession**

In Vermont soil I learned to want,
to press my thumb against the seed
and call the swelling fruit my own—
each tomato a red account
I balanced against my neighbor's need.

They came with baskets, hands held out,
as if the summer owed them share.
I gave. I smiled. I counted loss.
The vine grew heavy, and my doubt
grew heavier: *why must I be fair?*

I fasted then from generous things.
Locked the gate. Let the zucchini rot
rather than watch it feed a stranger.
Abstinence has its own dark springs—
the hoarding heart that wants and wants a lot.

But past the beans, against the wall
where frost should kill what will not bend,
I raised a fig in a barrel of clay,
dragged it to cellar come the fall—
my private Eden, mine to tend.

*This* I would keep. *This* was the prize
for all my labor, all my sweat.
Not common as the tomato's blush
but ancient, sacred, paradise—
a fruit the pharaohs coveted.

I told myself the fig was mine
by some deep law of worthiness,
that immortality was owed
to one who guarded root and vine,
who gave the world a little less.

And yet the fig, when at last it split,
was sweeter than I could consume.
It spilled its honey, seed and skin,
too much for one mouth to admit—
a hundred summers in one room.

I sat alone with what I'd won.
The sacred fruit, the guarded gate.
And something in the surplus stung:
that even hoarded, this abundance
was never mine to arbitrate.

The tomato asked to be given.
The fig, immortal, asked the same.
And I—so certain of my earning—
learned worthiness is not a wage
but something softer, without name:

the willingness to open hands
before the frost, before the fall,
to let the sweetness overflow
its barrel, its accounting, its demands—
to be, at last, deserving of it all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
